transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, well, I came in because... I don't know, my brain just feels like it completely stalls out on me. I work as an engineering technologist, so I'm at my computer a lot, and usually I'm really good at my job, you know, I got my bachelor's a few years ago and I know what I'm doing. But lately, it's like the gears just entirely grind to a halt. 

I'll sit there at my desk with a test report open, or even just a really simple CAD note that I need to add to a drawing, and I will literally just sit there for an entire hour. Just staring at the screen. And I can't decide what the next sentence should be, or even what checkbox I'm supposed to click. It's not that I don't understand the data or the schematics, it's just... I can't make the decision to actually type the words. I just stare at the blinking cursor and try to force myself to pick a direction, but my mind is just stuck. It's like a car engine that just keeps turning over but won't catch, and before I know it, half the morning is gone and I haven't written a single thing. It's just so frustrating because it should be automatic, but I just sit there paralyzed over a simple drop-down menu.
Did anything unusual or stressful happen before you started experiencing these episodes of feeling stuck?

Um, well, I guess... I mean, I wouldn't say it was unusual, because reassignments happen a lot in our division depending on project loads, but it was definitely a big transition. They moved me into a prototype-testing role. That was, well, about a year and a month ago. 

And before that, I was mostly just doing standard quality assurance on legacy components, which is super routine, you know? You just follow the established checklist, log any deviations in the system, and you're done for the day. It's very predictable. But prototype-testing is just... it's a completely different environment. You're looking at these alpha builds of hardware that have literally never been manufactured before, so there's no historical baseline to compare them to. You have to write the testing protocols almost entirely from scratch sometimes, which means a lot more responsibility. 

I was actually really excited when my manager first told me about the move, because it felt like they really trusted my judgment. I have my degree, I know the theory, so I told myself I should be able to handle it. But almost as soon as I started that position, right around thirteen months ago, that’s when this whole... this inability to just make a choice and do the work started. I'd be looking at a new circuit board, needing to set up the thermal stress parameters, and the pressure of not having a strict, pre-written guideline just... it completely overwhelmed me. So, yeah, this has been going on since I was moved into that prototype-testing role a year and a month ago. I just keep thinking about how if I had just stayed on the legacy parts, maybe my brain wouldn't be doing this, but they needed me on the new project, and now I just sit there wasting hours of the company's time because I can't pick a testing parameter.
Do you find yourself avoiding your work tasks or responsibilities in the prototype-testing role?

Yeah, um... I guess avoidance is one way to put it. It’s more like I just... I physically can’t make myself do them, so I end up putting them off, and it’s actually gotten really, really bad. Like, just recently, I completely missed a key project deadline. It was for this massive thermal validation report on a new sensor housing, and I knew about it for weeks. Every single day I told myself, "Okay, today I’m going to write the summary," but I just sat there. And because I missed that deadline, it’s like I’ve lost all my credibility. Now I have to have my coworkers double-check everything I do, or they even end up taking over parts of the reports entirely. Like, Sarah from the hardware team literally had to write the calibration section for me last week because I just couldn't get the words out. I used to finish these things completely on my own, no problem, usually ahead of schedule! Now I’m just this bottleneck, and I feel so guilty watching them pick up my slack because they have their own heavy workloads, you know? 

And the worst part is, it’s not even just at work anymore. You’d think when I clock out I’d feel some sort of relief, but it just bleeds into everything else. Outside of work, I have mostly just completely stopped seeing people. My friends keep texting me to go get coffee or come over for game nights—we used to do board game nights every other Friday—and I just leave them on read or make up some excuse about being too tired. I don't even do the normal routines that used to keep me steady anymore. I used to meal prep every Sunday, like clockwork, chopping vegetables and portioning things out so my week was organized, and I haven't done that in... I don't even know how long. I just go home and do nothing. My whole schedule, everything that kept me grounded, it's just gone.
Do you often feel anxious or worried about making mistakes in your prototype-testing role?

Anxious? I mean... yeah, but it's... it's almost more than just being worried about the mistake itself, if that makes sense. It’s like it takes over my entire identity. 

For example, just the other day, I was in the lab doing a basic voltage check on this new breadboard layout, and I accidentally swapped the positive and negative leads for like, maybe two seconds. It didn't short anything out, the overcurrent protection kicked in immediately, so there was literally no harm done, right? My manager didn't even see it. Anyone could do that. But I just... I couldn't let it go. I still can't. 

I just keep replaying these tiny, insignificant mistakes from the lab over and over and over in my head. And it’s not just me thinking, "Oh, I made a silly error, I need to be more careful next time." It turns into this huge, overwhelming spiral where I’m telling myself that I’m not just bad at this job, but that I’m actually just a bad person. Like, fundamentally broken and flawed. I’ll be sitting there at my desk, or lying in bed at 2 AM, just looping that two-second mistake, and thinking about how I shouldn't even have my bachelor's degree, how I must have tricked everyone into hiring me. 

And then I start thinking that I deserve whatever bad things happen to me. Like, I deserve whatever consequences come from it—if they fire me, or if my coworkers end up hating me, or if I just fail completely and lose everything. I tell myself I deserve it because I'm just... rotten on the inside, you know? It's not just a professional mistake to me anymore, it feels like a deep moral failure. Every single time I click the wrong cell in Excel or misread a tolerance limit by a fraction of a millimeter, it just proves to me that I'm completely worthless. And I know, logically, it sounds so dramatic to say a spreadsheet error makes me a terrible human being, but in the moment, and for hours and days afterward, it feels like absolute, undeniable fact. I just can't stop the loop of thinking how much I deserve to be punished for being so utterly incompetent...
Do you find yourself having repetitive, intrusive thoughts that you can't control?

Intrusive thoughts? Um... I mean, besides what I just told you about replaying my mistakes? Not really, no. 

Like, if you mean random things just popping into my head out of nowhere, I don't really get that. I know some people get those, like my roommate in college used to always think she left the front door unlocked and would have to go back and check it three times, or she'd get these weird random images in her head, but my brain doesn't really do that. If I haven't messed something up, I'm not really thinking about much at all. Actually, most of the time when I'm not at work, my mind is just... blank. Just really heavy and blank. Like I'll be sitting on the couch staring at the wall in my apartment and there's just nothing going on up there. 

It's only when I make an error—like the voltage check I mentioned, or if I format a report wrong for the engineering team—that the thoughts start looping. And even then, it doesn't feel like an "intrusive" thought, if that makes sense? It just feels like... the truth. It's just me focusing on the reality of how badly I messed up and what a failure I am. It's directly tied to something I actually did. 

But just random, uncontrollable thoughts that have nothing to do with anything? No, I definitely haven't noticed anything like that. I just sit there in the quiet most of the time. Well, quiet until I remember an email I sent with a typo or something, and then it's just the guilt spiral all over again. But yeah, no, nothing totally out of the blue like what you're asking about.
Have you been experiencing feelings of sadness or hopelessness most of the day, nearly every day?

Sadness? Um... I don't know if sadness is really the right word for it. When I think of being sad, I think of, you know, crying or feeling really heartbroken about something specific. Like when my family's golden retriever passed away when I was a freshman in college, I was completely devastated. I cried every single day for weeks, and I couldn't even look at a picture of him without tearing up. That felt like real, heavy sadness. But what I'm dealing with right now... it's not like that at all. I actually haven't cried in... gosh, I don't even know how long. Months, probably. 

It's more like I just don't feel much of anything. And as for feeling hopeless... I mean, hopelessness almost sounds like it requires energy, if that makes sense? Like you have to actively be looking at the future and despairing over it. But I don't even look at the future anymore. I just sort of... exist. Like I was saying earlier about sitting on the couch, it's just this massive, heavy blankness. 

Just last weekend, I tried to put on this movie that always, always makes me cry—it's this really touching story about a rescue dog—and I just sat there staring at the screen for two hours. Nothing. Not a single tear, not even a lump in my throat. My chest just felt like it was full of wet cement, but there was no actual emotion attached to it. So no, I wouldn't say I feel sad most of the day. It's more like the entire emotional part of my brain has just been unplugged. I just wake up, drag myself to the lab, try not to ruin any more prototype tests, come home, and stare at the wall. It's just a completely flat, gray baseline all the time. I keep thinking I probably should be sad, especially with how much I'm letting my team down, but the feeling itself just isn't there.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

Lost interest... yeah. Yeah, definitely. Actually, that's one of the things that really makes me realize how different everything is right now. 

Like, I have this 3D printer for miniatures at home. I used to be completely obsessed with it. I'd spend hours after work just calibrating the build plate, adjusting the exposure times down to the fraction of a second, you know, really dialing in the settings so the details on the little figures would come out perfectly crisp. It was such a fun puzzle for me. I was working on this one specific figure, this really intricate little fantasy character, and I was so excited to put it together and paint it. But... I don't know. I printed the first half of it, and it's just... it's been sitting there. Right there on the curing station. For months. 

Every time I walk past it in my apartment, I look at it and think, "I should finish that. I used to love doing this." But the thought of actually turning the machine on, pouring the resin, cleaning the vat... it just feels impossible. It's like my brain just completely rejects the idea of doing it. There's no spark, no motivation. 

And it's not just the technical hobbies, either. It's stuff that's supposed to be relaxing, too. I used to do yoga a few times a week. I had this whole routine where I'd unroll my mat by the window, and it felt so good to just stretch and breathe after being hunched over workbenches in the lab all day. Or I'd go for these long walks in the woods near my place on the weekends. I used to really, really look forward to those walks. Just being out in the trees, getting away from screens and circuits and everything. 

But now... if I even think about doing yoga, or putting on my boots to go out to the woods, it doesn't feel like something I actually *want* to do. It just feels like another task. Like another chore on this endless list of things I have to force myself through. I'll look at my yoga mat rolled up in the corner, and it just feels exhausting. The idea of walking in the woods just feels like I'd be dragging my heavy body around out there for no reason, just checking a box because it's something I'm "supposed" to do. There's no joy in it anymore. None at all. It's just more effort, and I don't have the energy for it. So I just... I just leave the printer off, and I leave the mat rolled up, and I go back to sitting on the couch.
Do you often find yourself being excessively critical of yourself when things don't go as planned?

Excessively critical... um, yeah. Yeah, that's... that's probably putting it mildly. 

I mean, I mentioned earlier about how I replay things, right? But it's... it's so much more than just realizing I made an error. I keep replaying these tiny, tiny mistakes from the lab. Like, a calibration being off by a fraction of a percent, or putting the wrong date format on a testing log, or that voltage check I was talking about. Things that, realistically, probably take two seconds to fix and no one else even remembers. But in my head, I just loop them endlessly. 

And the whole time I'm replaying it, I'm not just thinking about the technical mistake. I'm just telling myself that I'm not just bad at this job—which I clearly am, I mean, I'm a terrible engineering tech right now—but that I'm actually just a bad person. Like, fundamentally. Because a good person wouldn't be so careless, you know? A good person wouldn't drag the whole engineering team down with their stupidity. 

I'll just sit there on the couch, staring at the wall like I said, and I'll just dissect every little thing I did wrong that day, and it always leads back to this conclusion that I'm just a completely worthless human being. It's like my brain takes a typo in an email and turns it into proof that my entire character is flawed. And the worst part is, I feel like I absolutely deserve it. I feel like I deserve whatever consequences come from it. If my manager called me in tomorrow and fired me, or if everyone in the lab just stopped talking to me, I'd just accept it. I wouldn't even try to defend myself or apologize because I'd just think, "Yes, exactly, this is what I deserve for being such a failure." 

It's not just criticism, it's like this absolute certainty that I'm a fraud and a burden, and I deserve to be punished for every little misstep I make. So yeah, I guess I am critical, but it just feels like I'm finally seeing the truth about myself.
Do you often feel guilty about things that happen in your life?

Yeah, I mean... I guess that ties right into exactly what I was just saying a second ago. The guilt is... it's constant. It's completely tied to those tiny mistakes I keep replaying from the lab. 

When I mess up a calibration or put the wrong date format on a testing log, it's not just me being critical of the technical error, it's this overwhelming, crushing guilt that just swallows me whole. I'll sit there and I just tell myself over and over that I'm not just bad at this job—which I am, I'm doing terrible right now—but that I'm actually a fundamentally bad person. Because in my head, a good person wouldn't make those mistakes. A good person wouldn't burden their engineering team like that. I feel so incredibly guilty for even being there, like I'm tricking them or dragging down the whole project with my carelessness. 

And the guilt is so heavy that, like I was saying, I really feel like I deserve whatever consequences come from it. If my manager pulled me into an office and yelled at me, or if they just outright fired me, the guilt would just make me nod and say, "You're right, I'm awful, I deserve this." I wouldn't even try to explain myself. I just feel guilty for... for everything. For every little misstep, every fraction of a percent I'm off on a voltage check. It just proves to me that I'm a bad person who deserves to be punished, you know? It's just exhausting to feel that much guilt over a simple data log, but I can't turn it off. I just sit on the couch and let the guilt eat away at me for hours.
Have you ever experienced repetitive behaviors or mental acts that you felt driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly?

Um, repetitive behaviors... like, having to do something a certain number of times, or having strict rules? No, no, I don't have anything like that. 

I mean, I know I just spent all that time talking about how I replay those tiny mistakes from the lab, like the voltage checks or the date formats, and I guess you could say that's a mental thing that repeats. But it's not... it's not like a rule I have to follow, you know? It's not like I'm doing it on purpose to fix something or because I feel driven to perform a specific act to stop something bad from happening. It's just my brain attacking me. I don't *want* to be doing it. 

Actually, the idea of having rules or having to perform actions rigidly... that takes a kind of energy that I just absolutely do not have right now. Like I was saying before about the 3D printer and the yoga mat, I can barely get myself to do the basic things I used to actually enjoy, let alone some complicated set of rules I *have* to do. If there was a rule in my head that said I had to, I don't know, check the lock on my apartment door five times before I leave for the engineering building, I'd probably just never leave the apartment. Because honestly, even checking it once feels like climbing a mountain some days. 

Everything is just so heavy. I don't have the motivation to keep up with rigid routines. I just sit there on the couch. So, no, I don't have any rituals or compulsions or anything like that. The closest thing is just that constant loop of guilt and telling myself how useless I am, but that's not a rule I'm applying. It's just... it's just the reality of what's happening in my head all the time. I don't do anything *in response* to it, except maybe sink deeper into the cushions and just let it happen.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

Weight? Um, no, I don't... I don't think so. I haven't really noticed any significant weight loss. 

I mean, I don't really weigh myself very often anyway. I used to, back when I was actually going to yoga and trying to stay active, but lately, I just... I haven't even looked at the scale in my bathroom. It's just sitting there gathering dust. I guess my clothes still fit the same, mostly. Maybe my work pants are a little loose, but that could just be because they're old and stretched out from sitting at the lab bench all day. 

Honestly, eating has just become another chore, you know? It's like, I know I *should* eat, but the thought of actually getting up, going to the kitchen, figuring out what to make, cooking it, cleaning up afterward... it's just exhausting. Sometimes I'll just stare at the fridge and then go back to the couch because it's too much effort. Or I'll just eat whatever is easiest, like a handful of crackers or something, just so my stomach stops growling. But even then, I don't really enjoy it. Food just tastes like cardboard lately. 

But despite all that, I don't think I've actually dropped a bunch of weight. I'm probably just maintaining whatever I was at before all this started. I know some people lose a ton of weight when they're stressed or feeling like this, but I think my body is just... stagnant. Just like everything else in my life right now. So, no, to answer your question, no significant weight loss that I'm aware of. Just the same old me, taking up space.
Have you ever thought about harming yourself?

Harming myself... um... I mean, I don't sit at home and plan things out, you know? Like, I don't have a specific plan with, I don't know, pills or anything like that. But... well, the drive to the engineering building is about thirty minutes, mostly down this one long stretch of highway, and lately, the commute has just become really, really hard for me. 

When I'm in the car, just staring at the road and thinking about going into the lab and facing all those mistakes and that crushing guilt I was telling you about... I just catch myself thinking it would be so much easier if I just didn't arrive anywhere. Not just work, but anywhere at all. I'll be looking at the concrete divider, or the ditch off to the right, and my brain just starts telling me how simple it would be to just end the trip right there. Just... stop having to try so hard. 

And sometimes that idea—the thought of actually steering off the road into the barrier or down the embankment—it gets so real and it actually scares me. It scares me so much that I can feel my heart pounding, and I have to physically grip the steering wheel as hard as I possibly can, just white-knuckling it so my hands don't do something without my permission. And then I have to pull over. I just hit the blinker and pull off onto the shoulder and put my hazard lights on. 

I'll just sit there on the side of the highway for ten, maybe fifteen minutes, just gripping the wheel and crying, trying to fight off how appealing it sounds to just make everything stop. Because I don't think I actively want to die, but living is just so exhausting right now. Everything is so heavy. And the idea of just ending the commute forever... it's terrifying that it sounds like a relief. So I just sit there until I feel safe enough to put the car back in drive. It makes me late sometimes, and I just tell my manager there was traffic, which I guess is sort of true, it's just... a different kind of traffic. But yeah, those thoughts on the road... they happen a lot.
Have you ever experienced a period like this before in your life?

Have I experienced a period like this before? Um... well, no, not really. Not like this. I mean, sure, college was stressful, especially engineering classes, you know? There were times I was pulling all-nighters and feeling overwhelmed, but that was just normal stress. I could always bounce back. I'd ace a test or finish a project, and the heavy feeling would lift, and I'd go out with friends or go to yoga, and I'd feel like myself again.

But this... this is entirely different. This is a constant, suffocating weight that just doesn't lift. And it's been going on for a really long time now. I can actually pinpoint exactly when it started. It was about a year and a month ago, right when they moved me into the prototype-testing role at the lab. 

Before that, I was just doing standard quality assurance, and I was good at it. It was routine, predictable. But then they promoted me—which I thought was a good thing at first, you know? I thought it meant they trusted me. But the prototype testing... it's so much more pressure. Every little measurement, every voltage check, every material stress test... if I mess it up, it's not just a batch of standard parts that gets flagged, it's the whole new design. It's months of the engineers' work down the drain. 

And right around that time, a year and a month ago, when I first started that new role, that's when the guilt started creeping in. That's when I started replaying every single thing I did during the day, convinced I had ruined something. And then it just got worse and worse until I stopped going to yoga, stopped cooking, stopped... well, stopped wanting to even make the drive to the building. So, no, I've never felt like this before in my life. It's been this one long, terrible stretch ever since that job change thirteen months ago, and it just feels like it's never going to end.
Have you been avoiding social gatherings or meetings with friends and family because you feel anxious or uncomfortable around them?

Social gatherings... um, I don't... I don't really know if it's because I'm anxious or uncomfortable, exactly. I mean, I guess I have been avoiding people, but it's not like I'm having panic attacks about seeing them or anything like that. It's more just... I don't have the energy for it. 

Like, my friend Sarah, she's been trying to get me to go to this brunch place we used to love, the one downtown with the really good mimosa flights? She's texted me maybe four times in the last month about it, and every time I just make up some excuse about having to catch up on chores or being too tired from the lab. And my parents, they usually want me to come over for Sunday dinner, but I haven't been in weeks. I just tell them I'm not feeling well, which isn't entirely a lie, but it's not the flu or anything.

It's just that when I think about sitting across from them, or from Sarah, and having to smile and pretend everything is fine, or having to explain why I'm so exhausted all the time, or—even worse—having them ask about work... it just feels like climbing a mountain. I can't sit there and listen to them talk about their normal lives and their normal problems while my brain is just constantly telling me how useless I am and how I'm probably ruining everything at the lab. 

And if I go, I'll just bring them down, you know? I don't want to sit there and be a raincloud while they're trying to enjoy their weekend. So it's easier to just stay home on the couch. It's not that I'm scared of them, or anxious about the social interaction itself... it's just that the whole process of being around people and having to exist in their world is just too much right now. So I just don't do it. I just stay in my apartment.
Do you feel like your symptoms have been getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past few months?

Better, worse, or the same... um... gosh, I don't even really know how to answer that, to be honest. It’s... it’s like, when you’re in it every single day, it’s so hard to measure, you know? Because every morning I wake up and I stare at the ceiling for what feels like hours—even though it’s probably only twenty minutes before my alarm actually goes off—and I just feel that same exact dread. 

I mean, maybe there are days where the drive to work is slightly less terrifying, or maybe there's a day where I actually manage to eat a piece of toast instead of just drinking coffee until my stomach physically hurts. But does that mean it's getting better? I don't think so. It doesn't feel like progress, it just feels like a random fluke. And as for getting worse... I don't know if the guilt and the weight of it all *can* feel much heavier without me just completely collapsing right there on the lab floor. 

It's just this constant, flat, gray baseline that I've been stuck at for months now. Like I was saying earlier about the lab, ever since that promotion thirteen months ago, it just hit a certain point of awful and then it just... stayed there. Sometimes I try to look back and evaluate it, like, I'll ask myself, "Was I crying more in October than I am now?" or "Did I feel more useless testing the phase-one prototypes than I do with the current batch?" But I honestly can't tell you. The days just completely bleed into each other. 

I wake up, I go to work, I stress about ruining the engineers' designs, I drive home white-knuckling the steering wheel, I sit on the couch, I ignore Sarah's texts, and then I go to sleep and do it all over again. It's just a loop. A really, really exhausting loop where nothing ever really changes. It just feels like one long, unending Tuesday, if that makes any sense? You're just stuck in the middle of the week forever. So I guess... I guess I really don't know if there's been a shift. I haven't noticed one. It just feels exactly the same.
Have you ever thought about how you would harm yourself if you were to act on those thoughts about not arriving at your destination?

How I would do it... um... well, it's not like I sit at home on the couch and try to come up with a plan or write out a note or anything like that. It’s... it’s really just when I’m in the car. Like I was saying before about the drive to work being terrifying, that's exactly where it happens. 

I'll be on my commute, usually in the morning when I'm heading toward the lab, and the dread is just sitting so heavy on my chest, and I'll just be staring at the lines on the highway. And I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I just didn't arrive anywhere. Not at work, where I have to face the prototypes and the pressure, and not back home... just nowhere. Just a complete stop to all of it. 

And then... then the thought comes of how easy it would be to just jerk the steering wheel. Just a quick, sharp turn to the right, off the road and into the embankment or the trees. It’s just right there, that thought of how fast it could be over. 

But honestly? The idea of actually steering off the road... it scares me. It scares me so much that my heart just completely drops into my stomach. When that thought pops into my head and feels a little too real, that’s when I end up gripping the steering wheel so incredibly hard—that white-knuckling I mentioned earlier, that's exactly why I do it. I grip it like I'm trying to physically stop my own hands from moving. And sometimes the thought scares me so badly that I actually have to put my blinker on and pull over to the shoulder of the highway. I'll just sit there with cars flying past me, gripping the wheel, trying to convince myself that I'm safe and that I'm not going to do it. So, I do think about steering off the road, a lot, but the thought terrifies me enough that I have to pull over just to make sure I don't actually act on it.
Have you ever thought about how you would harm yourself if you were to act on those thoughts?

Um, I mean, like I was just saying a second ago, right? I hope I'm making sense, maybe I didn't explain it clearly enough just now. But it's... it's really just limited to the car. I don't sit in my apartment thinking about, you know, other ways to do it, or looking things up online. It's specifically and pretty much exclusively during that morning commute to the lab. 

I'll just be driving, looking at the road stretching out in front of me, and I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I just... didn't arrive anywhere. Not at the lab with all the prototypes, not back home, just... nowhere. And the specific thought of how to make that happen is always just steering off the road. Just yanking the wheel hard to the right and going into the embankment. 

But I want to be really clear—because the idea of actually doing it, of actually steering off the road, it genuinely scares me. It terrifies me so much that my stomach just drops. That's why I do that white-knuckle thing I was talking about. I grip the wheel so incredibly hard because it’s almost like I have to physically lock my own hands in place so they don't do it. And sometimes that idea scares me enough that I literally cannot keep driving. I have to put my blinker on and pull over to the shoulder of the highway. I'll just sit there with my hazards on, listening to the cars rush past me, just gripping the wheel and breathing until I know for sure I'm not going to act on it. So the thought is there, and it's loud, but it scares me enough that I pull over to stop it from happening.
Have you ever experienced an episode like this before in your life, prior to the current situation at work?

No... um, no, never. And I think... I think that's honestly a big part of why this is all so incredibly overwhelming for me right now, because I have absolutely no frame of reference for it. I've never felt anything even remotely close to this before in my entire life. 

I mean, sure, I’ve been stressed in the past, you know? When I was getting my bachelor's, there were definitely weeks during finals where I’d be up until three in the morning in the library, drinking terrible vending machine coffee and completely freaking out about passing my materials or circuits classes. But that was... that was just normal college stress. It had an end date. You take the exam, you sleep for fourteen hours, and then you wake up and you feel totally fine again. You go get dinner with your roommates, you laugh, you move on. You bounce back. 

But this? This is just completely different. Before I got that promotion thirteen months ago, I actually really liked my job at the lab. I liked being a technician. I liked setting up the testing equipment, I felt competent, I felt like I belonged there. If I made a minor mistake back then, it was just a mistake—I'd fix it and move on. It wasn't this... this catastrophic, heavy proof that I'm completely useless and ruining the engineers' designs. I never used to wake up dreading the day. I never used to stare at the ceiling feeling like there was a physical boulder sitting on my chest, pinning me to the mattress. 

And I definitely, definitely never had thoughts about driving my car off the highway into a ditch. That's all completely new, and it's terrifying because I don't recognize myself anymore. It really just started building up after I took that new role and the pressure of the phase-one prototypes hit, and then it just settled into this awful baseline I told you about, and now it's just... it's my whole life. So, no, looking back, I've never had a period like this. I was always a pretty steady, normal person. This whole flat, gray, exhausting loop... it feels like it just completely hijacked a brain that used to work perfectly fine.
